lessons.title: What Makes It a Real Skill

blocks.robotComment: It's less about finding magic words and more about actual craft. 🛠️
blocks.body: Prompt engineering is the practice of deliberately designing, testing, and refining instructions so an AI tool reliably produces the output you actually want — not just once, but consistently, across many different situations. It's a real, learnable skill, not a collection of secret phrases.

highlights.text: deliberately designing, testing, and refining instructions

blocks.body: Casual prompting is asking a question once and taking whatever comes back. Prompt engineering is different: it treats a prompt like something you build and improve on purpose, the same way you'd refine a recipe until it works every time, not just the one time you got lucky.

highlights.text: treats a prompt like something you build and improve on purpose

blocks.body: This matters most once you're reusing a prompt — a template you'll use repeatedly, or a prompt that needs to work well no matter what specific input someone gives it. A prompt that happens to work great for one example but falls apart on a slightly different input isn't actually a good prompt yet, it's a lucky first draft.

highlights.text: isn't actually a good prompt yet, it's a lucky first draft

blocks.question: What best distinguishes prompt engineering from just asking an AI tool a question?
options: Prompt engineering deliberately designs and tests a prompt for reliable results, not just a one-off answer
Prompt engineering requires knowing secret magic words
Prompt engineering only applies to image generators, not text tools
There is no real difference between the two
blocks.explanation: The core difference is deliberate design and testing for reliability, not any special vocabulary.

blocks.sentence: A prompt that works great on one example but falls apart on a slightly different input is best described as a lucky ___, not a finished, reliable prompt.
options: first draft
final product
system prompt
blocks.explanation: A prompt only really counts as reliable once it holds up across different inputs, not just the one it happened to be tested on.

blocks.statement: Prompt engineering is mainly about memorizing special phrases that unlock better AI responses.
blocks.explanation: It's a systematic practice of designing and testing instructions for reliability — not a set of secret phrases.

blocks.robotComment: Once you can name the parts, you can tune each one on purpose instead of just rewriting the whole thing and hoping. 🔍
blocks.body: A well-built prompt is really made of several separate parts, each doing its own job: the role (who or what perspective the tool should adopt), the task (the actual instruction — what to do), the context (background information it needs to do the task well), the format (how the output should be structured), and the constraints (limits — length, tone, what to avoid).

highlights.text: the role
the task
the context
the format
the constraints

blocks.body: You already used pieces of this — giving a tool a role and a format — back in the basics of using AI tools well. Prompt engineering just formalizes it: naming each part lets you improve one at a time instead of rewriting a whole prompt from scratch every time something's slightly off.

highlights.text: naming each part lets you improve one at a time

blocks.code:
Role:         "You are a patient tutor explaining this to a total beginner."
Task:         "Explain what compound interest is."
Context:      "The reader has never taken a finance or math class."
Format:       "Two short paragraphs, no bullet points."
Constraints:  "Do not use any formulas or jargon."
blocks.caption: Five separate, independently adjustable pieces — not one big blob of instructions.

blocks.body: Not every prompt needs all five parts spelled out explicitly — a simple, low-stakes request doesn't need a role or heavy constraints. But for anything you'll reuse, or anything where the output really needs to land a specific way, deliberately filling in each part is what separates a reliable prompt from a vague one.

highlights.text: deliberately filling in each part is what separates a reliable prompt from a vague one

blocks.question: In the anatomy of a prompt, what does the 'constraints' part actually specify?
options: Limits — like length, tone, or things the response should avoid
The background information the tool needs to know
Which persona or perspective the tool should adopt
The exact wording the response must repeat back
blocks.explanation: Constraints are the limits placed on the response — length, tone, what to avoid — separate from the task itself.

blocks.sentence: The part of a prompt that specifies who or what perspective the AI tool should adopt is called the ___.
options: role
format
constraint
blocks.explanation: Role is specifically about the persona or perspective the tool takes on, separate from the task, format, or constraints.

blocks.statement: Every single prompt needs its role, task, context, format, and constraints spelled out explicitly to be effective.
blocks.explanation: Simple, low-stakes requests often don't need all five parts — the anatomy matters most for prompts you'll reuse or that need to land precisely.

blocks.robotComment: One great answer proves a prompt CAN work. It doesn't prove it WILL, every time. 🎯
blocks.body: The real test of a prompt isn't whether it produced one great answer — it's whether it produces a good answer across a range of different, realistic inputs. A prompt that's only tested once is really just a hopeful guess wearing a finished-looking outfit.

highlights.text: a good answer across a range of different, realistic inputs

blocks.body: Testing a prompt against multiple inputs is what actually separates prompt engineering from casual prompting. If you're building a prompt that summarizes customer messages, try it on a short message, a long rambling one, and an angry one — not just the single clean example you first thought of.

highlights.text: Testing a prompt against multiple inputs

blocks.body: When a prompt fails on a new input, that failure is useful information, not just bad luck — it tells you exactly which part of the prompt's anatomy (task, context, format, constraints) needs to be tightened. Reliable prompts are built through this cycle of testing and adjusting, not written perfectly on the first try.

highlights.text: that failure is useful information, not just bad luck

blocks.question: Why is testing a prompt against several different, realistic inputs important?
options: One successful result doesn't prove the prompt is reliable across the range of inputs it'll actually face
It is only necessary for prompts used inside a company
It's an optional extra step that doesn't really affect prompt quality
A prompt that works once will always work on every future input
blocks.explanation: Reliability is about consistent performance across varied inputs, which one successful test can't demonstrate on its own.

blocks.sentence: When a prompt fails on a new input, that failure is useful ___ that points to exactly what needs tightening.
options: information
luck
coincidence
blocks.explanation: A failure tells you specifically which part of the prompt needs adjustment — it's diagnostic, not just bad luck.

blocks.statement: A prompt that produces one impressive result has already been proven reliable.
blocks.explanation: One good result only shows the prompt CAN work — reliability requires testing across a range of different inputs.

questions.question: What actually defines prompt engineering as a discipline?
options: Deliberately designing, testing, and refining a prompt for reliable results
Memorizing a fixed list of magic words
Only relevant to people who write code
Getting one lucky, impressive answer

questions.statement: Casual prompting and prompt engineering are exactly the same thing.

questions.sentence: A prompt that only worked once, on one input, is really just a hopeful ___ dressed up as a finished prompt.
options: guess
certainty
contract

questions.question: Which of these is one of the five parts in a prompt's anatomy?
options: Context — the background information the tool needs
The file size of the response
The device the tool runs on
The internet speed of the user

questions.statement: Naming the separate parts of a prompt lets you improve one part at a time instead of rewriting the whole thing.

questions.sentence: Limits on a response — like length, tone, or things to avoid — are called ___.
options: constraints
tokens
endpoints

questions.question: What is the best way to check whether a prompt is actually reliable?
options: Test it against several different, realistic inputs, not just one
Ask it the exact same question twice in a row
Assume any prompt that sounds polite will work
Check how long the prompt is in characters

questions.statement: Every prompt, no matter how simple or low-stakes, needs role, task, context, format, and constraints all spelled out explicitly.

questions.sentence: When a prompt fails on a new input, that failure is useful ___ pointing to what needs to be tightened.
options: information
noise
randomness

questions.question: What is the relationship between prompt engineering and the basic prompting habits (specificity, roles, format) from using AI tools well?
options: Prompt engineering builds on and formalizes those same basics into a systematic, testable practice
They are completely unrelated skills
Prompt engineering replaces the need for specificity entirely
Basic prompting habits only apply to image generators

lessons.title: The Two Layers: System and User

blocks.robotComment: Think of it as your AI's personality settings versus today's to-do item. 🎭
blocks.body: Every conversation with an AI tool actually runs on two separate layers of instruction. The persistent layer — often called a system prompt or custom instructions — is set once and quietly applies to every single message you send afterward. The user layer is the specific message you type each time: the one-off request for whatever you need right now.

highlights.text: two separate layers of instruction
The persistent layer
The user layer

blocks.body: Many consumer AI tools include a settings area where you can write a persistent instruction once, and it then applies automatically to every conversation from then on — things like 'always respond in French' or 'keep answers under 100 words' or 'never use bullet points.' You never have to retype it, and you don't even have to remember it's there.

highlights.text: applies automatically to every conversation from then on

blocks.body: The user message, by contrast, is where the specific, changing details live: 'summarize this email,' 'write a caption for this photo,' 'debug this error message.' The persistent instruction stays constant in the background; the user message is what's actually different every single time you use the tool.

highlights.text: is where the specific, changing details live
what's actually different every single time

blocks.code:
Persistent instruction (set once, in settings):
  "Always respond in a warm, encouraging tone. Keep answers under 150 words. Never use jargon without explaining it."

User message (typed fresh, this one time):
  "Explain why my sourdough starter isn't rising."
blocks.caption: The persistent layer sets the ongoing rules. The user message is the actual, one-off ask.

blocks.question: Which of these best describes what a persistent (system-level) instruction does?
options: It quietly applies to every future conversation until you change it
It only affects the single message you send it with
It replaces the need to ever type a user message
It resets itself after every conversation
blocks.explanation: A persistent instruction is set once and continues applying automatically to future conversations, unlike a one-off user message.

blocks.sentence: The one-off, specific request you type for a given task is called the ___ message, as opposed to the persistent instruction.
options: user
system
constraint
blocks.explanation: The user message is the changing, task-specific request; the persistent instruction is the stable, ongoing layer.

blocks.statement: A persistent instruction needs to be retyped every single time you send a new message.
blocks.explanation: That's the opposite of the point — a persistent instruction is set once and applies automatically afterward without retyping.

blocks.robotComment: One question sorts almost every instruction into the right bucket. 🗂️
blocks.body: The practical test for which layer something belongs in is simple: will this rule apply to basically every future request, or is it specific to what you need right now? Tone, formatting defaults, and standing rules belong in the persistent layer. The specific topic, the actual content to work with, and one-time details belong in the user message.

highlights.text: will this rule apply to basically every future request, or is it specific to what you need right now

blocks.body: Say you want a coding assistant to always explain its reasoning before giving code, always use a specific programming language unless told otherwise, and never apologize excessively. Those are standing rules — they belong in the persistent instruction. But 'write a function that sorts this list' is a one-time task — it belongs in the user message, every time, because it's different every time.

highlights.text: Those are standing rules
it's different every time

blocks.body: Mixing the two up creates two different problems. Stuff a persistent instruction full of details for last Tuesday's specific task, and it keeps applying that irrelevant detail to everything else you ask forever. Leave a standing rule out of the persistent layer and put it only in one user message, and you'll have to remember to retype it every single time — or forget, and get inconsistent results.

highlights.text: it keeps applying that irrelevant detail to everything else you ask forever
you'll have to remember to retype it every single time

blocks.code:
Wrong (task detail stuck in the persistent layer):
  "Always format responses as a numbered list, and today the topic is quarterly sales figures."

Right (rule persists, task moves to the user message):
  Persistent: "Always format responses as a numbered list."
  User: "Summarize this quarter's sales figures."
blocks.caption: A standing rule stays put. A one-time detail travels with the request that needs it.

blocks.question: Which of these is a standing rule that belongs in a persistent instruction rather than a one-off user message?
options: Always respond in a formal tone
Summarize this specific article about coral reefs
Translate this one sentence into Spanish
Fix the bug in this particular code snippet
blocks.explanation: A tone rule applies to every future request, which is exactly what belongs in the persistent layer — the other options are one-time, task-specific requests.

blocks.sentence: A rule that should apply to basically every future request, like a default tone or format, belongs in the ___ layer.
options: persistent
user
constraint
blocks.explanation: Rules meant to apply broadly and repeatedly belong in the persistent layer, not repeated in every user message.

blocks.statement: Putting a one-time, task-specific detail into a persistent instruction is a good way to keep it handy for future requests.
blocks.explanation: A one-time detail stuck in the persistent instruction keeps getting applied to unrelated future requests, which usually isn't what you want.

blocks.body: Deciding where an instruction belongs comes down to one question: would you want this rule active for every future conversation, or does it only make sense for what you're asking right now? If the answer is 'every time,' it belongs in the persistent layer. If the answer is 'just this once,' it belongs in the user message.

highlights.text: would you want this rule active for every future conversation, or does it only make sense for what you're asking right now

blocks.body: Not every tool gives you a separate settings field for a persistent instruction. Even then, the two-layer thinking still helps: you can open a single prompt with your standing preferences, then follow with the specific task, so the two layers are still separated — just inside the same message instead of two different fields.

highlights.text: the two-layer thinking still helps

blocks.robotComment: A well-run assistant is basically a stable rulebook plus a stream of different questions. 📋
blocks.body: In practice, a good setup combines both layers on purpose. A support-reply assistant might have a persistent instruction covering tone, a standard closing line, and a length limit — while each user message supplies the actual customer complaint that changes every time. Neither layer tries to do the other's job.

highlights.text: Neither layer tries to do the other's job

blocks.code:
Persistent instruction: "Always be empathetic and concise. End every reply with a note that help is available."

User message #1: "Customer says their order arrived damaged."
User message #2: "Customer says they were charged twice."
blocks.caption: One stable persistent instruction, reused across many different one-off user messages.

blocks.question: A team wants every reply from their AI assistant to always include a disclaimer and use a formal tone, no matter what the specific question is. Where should that rule live?
options: In the persistent instruction, since it applies to every future request
Retyped into every single user message
It cannot be set up in advance at all
In the format section of just one lucky prompt
blocks.explanation: A rule that should apply to every future request belongs in the persistent layer, so it does not need to be retyped each time.

blocks.sentence: The simplest test for where an instruction belongs is asking whether it should apply to every future request or just the ___ one.
options: current
persistent
formal
blocks.explanation: If a rule only makes sense for the immediate task, it belongs in the user message, not the persistent layer.

blocks.statement: Even in tools without a separate persistent-instruction setting, it can still help to structure one prompt with standing preferences first and the specific task after.
blocks.explanation: The two-layer idea still applies inside a single prompt, even when a tool has no dedicated system-prompt field.

lessons.title: What Makes a Persistent Instruction Useful

blocks.robotComment: The best persistent instructions are boring on purpose — that's what makes them reliable. 🧱
blocks.body: A persistent instruction earns its place by covering things that should genuinely hold true across every request: a default tone, a standard output format, a language preference, or a short list of things to always avoid. These are the settings you would otherwise have to repeat in every single message.

highlights.text: a default tone, a standard output format, a language preference, or a short list of things to always avoid

blocks.body: Good candidates read the same no matter what the actual task turns out to be: 'always explain acronyms on first use,' 'never recommend a specific brand,' 'default to metric units unless asked otherwise,' 'keep responses under 200 words.' None of these depend on knowing what the next request will be about.

highlights.text: None of these depend on knowing what the next request will be about

blocks.body: A useful way to test a candidate rule is to imagine it attached to ten completely unrelated future requests — one about a recipe, one about a code bug, one about a vacation itinerary. If the rule still makes sense every time, it belongs in the persistent layer. If it only makes sense for one of those ten, it belongs in that one user message instead.

highlights.text: If the rule still makes sense every time, it belongs in the persistent layer

blocks.code:
Good persistent instruction candidates:
  - Always respond in plain, jargon-free language
  - Default to bullet points for anything with more than three items
  - Never make up a fact you are not confident about
  - Keep a warm but professional tone
blocks.caption: Each line still makes sense no matter what the next request turns out to be about.

blocks.question: Which of these is the best candidate for a persistent instruction?
options: Always keep responses under 150 words
Summarize the attached quarterly report
Translate this specific paragraph into German
List three restaurants near this one address
blocks.explanation: A length rule applies no matter what the topic is, which is exactly the kind of stable rule a persistent instruction should hold.

blocks.sentence: A good persistent instruction should still make sense no matter what the next ___ turns out to be about.
options: request
constraint
role
blocks.explanation: A rule that only makes sense for one specific topic is not a good fit for the persistent layer — it should hold up across unrelated requests.

blocks.statement: A persistent instruction should generally contain rules that would make sense attached to almost any future request.
blocks.explanation: That universality is exactly what separates a good persistent-instruction candidate from a one-off task detail.

lessons.title: What Doesn't Belong in a Persistent Instruction

blocks.body: Just as important as knowing what belongs in a persistent instruction is knowing what doesn't. Anything that changes from request to request — the actual subject matter, the specific document, the particular question — has no business living in the persistent layer, because it will be wrong or irrelevant the very next time you use the tool.

highlights.text: has no business living in the persistent layer

blocks.body: The name of today's client, the specific paragraph you need rewritten, the particular error message you're debugging, the exact recipe you're adapting — these are all one-time details. They belong in the user message precisely because next time they'll be completely different.

highlights.text: they'll be completely different

blocks.robotComment: A persistent instruction with a stray one-time detail in it is like a sticky note that never gets thrown away. 🗒️
blocks.body: Bury a one-time detail inside the persistent layer, and it silently attaches itself to every unrelated future request. Ask an AI tool to 'always compare this to last year's Q3 numbers,' set as a persistent instruction, and it'll keep trying to bring up Q3 numbers even when you're asking about something totally unrelated six months later.

highlights.text: it'll keep trying to bring up Q3 numbers even when you're asking about something totally unrelated

blocks.code:
Belongs only in a user message (changes every time):
  - The specific email you want rewritten
  - The meeting agenda for today
  - The complaint from this one customer
  - The particular code file with the bug
blocks.caption: Each of these is different tomorrow. None of them belong in a rule meant to persist.

blocks.question: Why is a specific one-time detail, like the exact document you want summarized today, a bad fit for a persistent instruction?
options: It will be irrelevant or wrong the next time you use the tool for something else
Persistent instructions cannot contain any nouns
It makes the persistent instruction too short
One-time details actually work fine as persistent instructions
blocks.explanation: A persistent instruction keeps applying to every future request, so a detail specific to just one task becomes irrelevant, or actively wrong, afterward.

blocks.sentence: A detail that changes every time you use a tool, like the exact document to summarize, belongs in the ___ message, not the persistent instruction.
options: user
system
format
blocks.explanation: One-time, task-specific details belong in the user message, since the persistent layer applies to every future request.

blocks.statement: It is fine to put a one-time task detail into a persistent instruction, since you can always delete it later.
blocks.explanation: Even though it can technically be deleted later, it keeps silently attaching itself to every request in the meantime, which usually causes confusing results.

blocks.robotComment: More rules doesn't mean more control — past a point, it means more contradictions. ⚖️
blocks.body: A persistent instruction can also fail in the opposite direction: by trying to do too much. Stack up enough rules — tone, format, length, forbidden topics, five different edge cases — and the instruction starts working against itself. Rules quietly contradict each other, and the tool has to guess which one wins.

highlights.text: by trying to do too much
the tool has to guess which one wins

blocks.body: Imagine a persistent instruction that says 'always be extremely concise,' 'always explain your reasoning in detail,' and 'always include a friendly greeting and sign-off.' Concise and detailed reasoning already pull in opposite directions, and now there's a greeting eating into the length budget too. The result is inconsistent — sometimes short, sometimes long, rarely quite right.

highlights.text: already pull in opposite directions

blocks.body: The fix is discipline, not more rules: keep a persistent instruction to a small number of genuinely important, non-conflicting points. If two rules ever compete, decide which one actually matters more and drop or soften the other, rather than piling on a third rule to referee between them.

highlights.text: keep a persistent instruction to a small number of genuinely important, non-conflicting points

blocks.code:
Overloaded: "Be concise. Be thorough. Always use bullet points. Never use bullet points for lists under three items. Always sound casual. Always sound professional. Include a greeting. Skip pleasantries and get straight to the point."

Lean: "Be concise and direct. Use a professional but warm tone. Skip greetings and get straight to the answer."
blocks.caption: The overloaded version contradicts itself at least twice. The lean version does not.

blocks.question: What typically happens when a persistent instruction is stacked with too many, sometimes conflicting, rules?
options: The results become inconsistent because the tool has to guess which rule takes priority
The tool automatically resolves every conflict perfectly every time
Extra rules always make output more reliable, with no downside
The persistent instruction stops working entirely
blocks.explanation: Contradictory or excessive rules make the output inconsistent, since the tool has no clear way to know which instruction should win.

blocks.sentence: When two rules in a persistent instruction genuinely conflict, the better fix is to drop or soften one of them rather than adding a third rule to ___ between them.
options: referee
translate
summarize
blocks.explanation: Adding more rules to resolve a conflict usually makes an overloaded instruction worse, not better — trimming down works better.

blocks.statement: Adding more and more rules to a persistent instruction always makes the output more reliable.
blocks.explanation: Past a certain point, more rules increase the chance of contradiction, which makes output less consistent, not more.
